meta.title: Who really said "Alas, poor Yorick, I knew him well"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shakespeare wrote the line — but Hamlet says “I knew him, Horatio.” The famous “I knew him well” is a later corruption.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Alas, poor Yorick, I knew him well'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a fake — a misquote. Hamlet’s words are “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (Act 5, Scene 1, first printed 1603).

answer.label: Shakespeare’s line — but misquoted
answer.sourceLine: The line really is Shakespeare’s — Hamlet in the graveyard, Hamlet Act 5, Scene 1, holding the skull of the court jester — but the words are not these. The 1603 first quarto reads “alas poore Yoricke I knew him Horatio,” and standard editions print “I knew him, Horatio”; “well” is a later popular corruption.

source.heading: The line as it was printed

source.excerpt: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio: a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy: he hath borne me on his back a thousand times; and now, how abhorred in my imagination it is! my gorge rises at it.
trail: The earliest printed text of the play already has the real words: the 1603 first quarto reads “alas poore Yoricke I knew him Horatio” in the Internet Shakespeare Editions old-spelling transcription ↗.

Standard modern-spelling editions agree. The graveyard scene at Shakespeare Online ↗, following K. Deighton’s Macmillan edition, prints “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio: a fellow of infinite jest”; Wikiquote’s sourced Act V, Scene i ↗ is the same.

Reference works name the error directly: the phrase history at Phrases.org.uk ↗ says the line “is often misquoted” as “I knew him well,” and Oxford’s quotations team calls “I knew him, Horatio” the textually correct reading ↗.
The publication history is documented: an unauthorised 1603 quarto, an authorised 1604 quarto “newly imprinted and enlarged,” and the 1623 Folio, per Hamlet: The Texts ↗.
source.excerptNote: The four words everyone remembers — “I knew him well” — are not in the speech. What gets dropped is the name of the man Hamlet is speaking to.

source.rightsNote: Hamlet was first printed in 1603, reprinted in an enlarged quarto dated 1604 and collected in the 1623 First Folio — all far earlier than the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so the text of the play is free to quote. The variant “I knew him well” has no identifiable author or claimant; individual modern editions do carry their own editorial matter, so we quote from a pre-1931 edited text.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: The man who wrote the other version
author.bio: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) is the most quoted writer in English, which is exactly why so many lines circulate in shapes he never wrote. Hamlet reached print in three early versions — an unauthorised quarto of 1603, an enlarged quarto of 1604, and the 1623 First Folio — and the graveyard speech survives in all of them as a private aside to one man standing beside Hamlet: Horatio. The skull-in-hand image became the single most reproduced picture of an actor in the role, and the caption travelled faster than the text.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong words
misattribution.intro: This is the rare case where the famous name is correct and the famous wording is not. Nobody else wrote the line; the corruption happened inside the quotation itself.

items.why: The word Hamlet actually says is a name, not an adverb. Phrase historians note the line “is often misquoted” in this form, against the real reading “I knew him Horatio” ↗, and the 1603 quarto already prints “alas poore Yoricke I knew him Horatio” ↗.

items.who: Cut stage versions with no Horatio
items.why: Oxford’s quotations editors observe that “I knew him well” may not be simply a failure of memory: it has been pointed out that in some heavily cut versions of Hamlet the character of Horatio was excised, and the variant could have derived from the memory of such a performance ↗. That is offered as a possibility, not a documented origin.

A lithograph by William Newman, published by G.S. Tregear at 96 Cheapside, is titled “Hamlet alas poor Yorick! I knew him well” and is catalogued by Yale’s Lewis Walpole Library as [1840?] ↗. The misquote long predates social media.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare wrote the line; he did not write “well.” The sourced text, in Wikiquote’s Act V, Scene i, reads “I knew him, Horatio” ↗.

context.heading: Why the wrong version wins
lead: Hamlet is not making a speech to an audience here. A gravedigger tosses up a skull, names it as the king’s old jester, and Hamlet turns to the friend standing next to him: “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio.” The name is the point — it fixes the moment as one man telling another that the clown who carried him on his back is now a lump of bone in his hand.

Swap “Horatio” for “well” and the line stops belonging to the play. It becomes portable: a caption for any dead thing, sayable by anyone holding anything. As Jem Bloomfield notes of the change, the alteration has the advantage of decontextualising the line ↗ — which is also a fair description of why it spread.
context.detailsSummary: The three early texts, and where the corruption shows up
detailsBody: The Internet Shakespeare Editions summary of the early texts records an unauthorised first quarto of 1603, an authorised second quarto dated 1604 (some copies 1605) “newly imprinted and enlarged,” and the 1623 First Folio, set from a scribal manuscript — see Hamlet: The Texts ↗. The 1603 quarto, the shortest and strangest of the three, already has “I knew him Horatio.”

The corrupted wording was in print culture a long time before the internet: Yale’s Lewis Walpole Library holds a lithograph titled “Hamlet alas poor Yorick! I knew him well,” published by G.S. Tregear at 96 Cheapside and catalogued as [1840?] ↗. We make no claim that this is the earliest instance — only that it is a dated, catalogued one.
